mustKnow: A converging (convex) lens is fat in the middle and brings parallel rays to the principal focus
A diverging (concave) lens is thin in the middle and spreads parallel rays apart
The focal length is the distance from the optical centre to the principal focus
The distant-object method: distant object, screen moved until sharp, lens-to-screen distance measured
A mean leaves out any anomalous reading

notOnThisSpec: Magnification as a calculation (image height divided by object height)
The power of a lens in dioptres
The eye, long sight and short sight and their correction

mustBeAbleTo: Name a lens as converging or diverging from its shape and from its ray-diagram symbol
Describe what each kind of lens does to rays arriving parallel to the principal axis
Label the principal axis, the optical centre, the principal focus and the focal length
For a converging lens, define the focal length by naming the two points it runs between
Say where the principal focus of a diverging lens is and how it is found
Describe the distant-object method and name the apparatus it uses
Explain why the object has to be distant, in terms of parallel rays
Spot an anomalous reading and take a mean without it
Say that a real image can be caught on a screen, and why

Lenses open with a picture and a one-mark naming question, then the definition of focal length, then the three-item method. Summer 2025 Foundation Q3(a) gave three marks for that method. Unit 7 Physics Booklet B has set the focal-length definition, the screen needed for a real image, and a mean with an anomalous reading in it.

noteBlocks.lede: A lens is a piece of glass with curved faces, and every ray that crosses it is refracted twice. One shape brings light together; the other spreads it apart. Which one you have, and how strongly it bends light, is the whole of this topic.

Define focal length using the principal focus and the centre of the lens
Measure a focal length with a distant object, a screen and a metre rule

noteBlocks.md:
A **converging** lens (also called convex) is **fat in the middle**. A **diverging** lens (concave) is **thin in the middle**.
In a ray diagram you never draw the curved glass. You draw a straight vertical line with arrowheads: **outwards** for converging, **inwards** for diverging. The arrowheads are the only thing that tells the two apart on paper.

noteBlocks.explain: Fat in the middle converges. It is worth saying the two words together every time, because swapping them is the commonest slip on this topic.

noteBlocks.md:
Send in rays that are **parallel to the principal axis** and a converging lens brings them all to one point. That point is the **principal focus**, written **F**.
The distance between the **centre of the lens** and the principal focus is the **focal length**. A fatter lens bends light more, so its focal length is shorter.

noteBlocks.title: Why parallel rays, and not any old rays?
noteBlocks.md: Because only parallel rays all meet at the same point. Rays from a nearby object arrive spread out and meet somewhere else, further from the lens — which is why the focal length is defined for parallel rays, and why the practical uses a distant object.

noteBlocks.prompt: Rays arriving parallel to the principal axis of a converging lens all pass through one point on the axis. What is that point called? (two words)
noteBlocks.answer: principal focus | the principal focus | principal focal point
noteBlocks.explain: The principal focus, marked F on every diagram. CCEA examiners have reported candidates not knowing where to label it.

noteBlocks.md:
A diverging lens spreads parallel rays apart. They never meet, so its principal focus is found by tracing the spreading rays **backwards** until the dashed lines cross, on the **same side as the light came from**.
CCEA asks you to tell the two lenses apart, and to define the focal length for a **converging** lens. Ray diagrams for diverging lenses are not on this specification.

noteBlocks.title: What examiners have written about the two lenses
noteBlocks.md: **Summer 2024 Foundation Q2:** a significant minority got converging and diverging **the wrong way round**. **Summer 2023 Foundation Q8** and **Higher Q3** found the opposite — most candidates did recognise a concave, diverging lens, so the naming itself is learnable.

noteBlocks.prompt: A lens is thin in the middle and thick at its edges. What happens to rays that arrive parallel to its principal axis?
options: they spread apart, as though coming from a point on the near side
they meet at a point on the far side
they carry straight on without bending
noteBlocks.answer: they spread apart, as though coming from a point on the near side
noteBlocks.explain: Thin in the middle diverges. The rays spread, and the point they seem to come from is on the same side as the incoming light.

noteBlocks.md:
The **principal axis** is the horizontal line through the middle of the lens. The **optical centre** is the point where it crosses the lens. **F** is marked on **both** sides, the same distance out each way.
So the definition you write is: the focal length is the distance between the **centre of the lens** and the **principal focus**.

noteBlocks.prompt: Complete the definition. A converging lens's focal length is the distance from the principal focus to the __ of the lens. (two words)
noteBlocks.answer: optical centre | centre | the optical centre
noteBlocks.explain: The optical centre. A Unit 7 Booklet B question gave a mark for these two words, and candidates could not recall them.

noteBlocks.md:
**Question.** Three measurements of lens-to-screen distance are 14.8 cm, 15.1 cm, 14.9 cm, and a fourth reading of 19.4 cm. Find the focal length.
**Step 1** — spot the odd one out: 19.4 cm is far from the other three, so it is anomalous and is left out.
**Step 2** — add the three that agree and divide by three.
**Answer** — the focal length is 14.9 cm.

noteBlocks.prompt: A student's lens-to-screen readings are 9.4 cm, 9.6 cm, 9.5 cm and 13.1 cm. Ignoring the anomalous reading, what is the focal length in cm, to one decimal place?
noteBlocks.explain: 13.1 cm is the anomaly, so leave it out: (9.4 + 9.6 + 9.5) ÷ 3 = 9.5 cm. Including an anomalous result in a mean has cost marks in Booklet B twice.

noteBlocks.md:
Name a lens as converging or diverging from its shape and from its symbol.
Say what each lens does to rays arriving parallel to the principal axis.
Define the focal length as the distance from the optical centre to the principal focus.
Describe the distant-object method and take a mean that leaves an anomaly out.

This usually opens with a picture of a lens or its symbol and one mark for naming it, then the definition of focal length, then three marks for the method: a **distant object**, a **screen** moved until the image is sharp, and the **lens-to-screen distance** measured. If you are stuck on the definition, name the two points it runs between. If a set of readings has an odd one out, leave it out of the mean and say why.

workedExamples.stem: A lens is thin in the middle and thick at its edges. Name it, say what it does to parallel rays, and state where its principal focus lies.

steps.working: Thin in the middle, thick at the edges: this is a diverging lens, also called concave.
steps.decision: Naming it first fixes everything else, and swapping the two names is the commonest slip on this topic.

options: because a lens thin in the middle spreads light out
because a lens thin in the middle brings light together
because the name depends on the glass, not the shape
whyMenu.explain: The shape decides it. Fat in the middle converges; thin in the middle diverges.

steps.working: Rays arriving parallel to the principal axis are spread apart as they pass through.
steps.decision: They never cross, so there is no point on the far side where they all meet.

steps.working: Trace the spreading rays backwards with dashed lines. Those lines cross at one point.
steps.decision: That point is the principal focus, and it lies on the same side as the light came from.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: It is a diverging (concave) lens. It spreads parallel rays apart, and its principal focus is the point on the near side where the backward extensions of those rays cross.

items.stem: Light passes from air into a piece of glass. What happens to its speed?
items.skill: Recalling the change of speed from refraction

options.text: it slows down
options.feedback: Yes, and that is why it changes direction.

options.text: it speeds up
options.feedback: Light is slower in glass than in air, which is why it bends towards the normal on the way in.

options.text: it stays the same
options.feedback: If the speed did not change there would be no refraction at all.

items.stem: A lens has two curved faces, so a ray crossing it is refracted how many times?
items.skill: Counting the boundaries a ray crosses

options.text: twice, once at each face
options.feedback: Yes. That is why the shape of both faces matters.

options.text: once, in the middle
options.feedback: Refraction happens at a boundary between two materials, and a lens has two of them.

options.text: not at all, because glass is transparent
options.feedback: Transparent means the light gets through, not that it carries straight on.

items.stem: Three readings of the same quantity are 6.1 cm, 6.3 cm and 9.8 cm. Which is the anomalous one?

options.text: 9.8 cm
options.feedback: Yes. It sits far outside the group the others form.

options.text: 6.1 cm
options.feedback: 6.1 cm is close to 6.3 cm, so it belongs with the group.

options.text: none of them, because all readings count
options.feedback: A reading well outside the rest is anomalous and is left out of a mean.

items.stem: Which shape of lens brings parallel rays together?

options.text: one that is fat in the middle
options.feedback: Yes: fat in the middle converges.

options.text: one that is thin in the middle
options.feedback: Thin in the middle spreads the rays apart, so that is the diverging lens.

options.text: one with two flat faces
options.feedback: A block with flat parallel faces shifts a ray sideways but does not bring rays together.

options.text: either, depending on which way round it is held
options.feedback: Turning a lens round does not change whether it converges. The shape decides it.

items.stem: Which two points does the focal length of a converging lens run between?

options.text: the optical centre of the lens and the principal focus
options.feedback: Yes, and both names are worth a mark.

options.text: the lens and the screen, whatever the object distance
options.feedback: Lens to screen is only the focal length when the object is distant, so the rays arrive parallel.

options.text: the object and the lens
options.feedback: That is the object distance, which changes as the object moves.

options.text: the two principal focuses on either side
options.feedback: That distance is twice the focal length.

items.stem: The symbol for a lens is a vertical line with arrowheads. Which symbol shows a diverging lens?

options.text: the one with the arrowheads pointing inwards
options.feedback: Yes. Inward arrowheads mean diverging.

options.text: the one with the arrowheads pointing outwards
options.feedback: Outward arrowheads are the converging symbol.

options.text: the one drawn with a dashed line
options.feedback: Dashed lines mean construction lines or a virtual image, not the kind of lens.

options.text: neither: the symbols are the same
options.feedback: The arrowheads are exactly what tells them apart on paper.

items.stem: Why must the object be a long way away when you measure a focal length this way?
items.skill: The reason behind the distant-object method

options.text: so that the light arriving at the lens is almost parallel
options.feedback: Yes, and parallel rays are the ones that meet at the principal focus.

options.text: so that the image on the screen is brighter
options.feedback: A distant object gives a dimmer image, not a brighter one. The reason is that its light arrives parallel.

options.text: so that the image is bigger and easier to measure
options.feedback: A distant object gives a small image. What matters is that its rays arrive parallel.

options.text: so that the lens does not get hot
options.feedback: Heat is not the issue here; the parallel rays are.

items.stem: Four lens-to-screen readings are taken and one is clearly out of line. What should be done with it?

options.text: leave it out and take the mean of the others
options.feedback: Yes. That is exactly the step Booklet B candidates have missed twice.

options.text: include it, because every reading is evidence
options.feedback: An anomalous reading pulls the mean away from the true value, so it is left out.

options.text: use it on its own, because it is the most recent
options.feedback: One reading is never better than the mean of the readings that agree.

options.text: halve it and then include it
options.feedback: There is no reason to halve a reading. It is either kept as it is or left out as an anomaly.

items.stem: Lens P has a focal length of 5 cm and lens Q has a focal length of 20 cm. Which statement is true?
items.skill: Linking focal length to how strongly a lens bends light

options.text: lens P is fatter in the middle and bends light more
options.feedback: Yes. A shorter focal length means the rays are brought together sooner.

options.text: lens Q is fatter in the middle and bends light more
options.feedback: Lens Q takes four times as far to bring rays together, so it bends each one less.

options.text: lens P must be a diverging lens
options.feedback: Both have a focal length and both can be converging; the number only says how strongly each bends light.

options.text: they bend light by the same amount
options.feedback: A focal length of 5 cm and one of 20 cm are very different strengths.

parts.stem:
Look at the two lenses in the figure.
Identify the converging lens.

options.text: the lens that is fat in the middle and thin at its edges
options.feedback: Correct. Fat in the middle brings rays together.

options.text: the lens that is thin in the middle and thick at its edges
options.feedback: That one spreads rays apart, so it is the diverging lens.

options.text: both of them, because all lenses bend light inwards
options.feedback: Both bend light, but only one bends it inwards. A lens thin in the middle spreads light out.

scheme.for: the lens that is fat in the middle (convex)

hints: Think about which shape makes the light meet.
parts.workedSolution: The lens that is fat in the middle. A converging lens (also called convex) brings parallel rays together at the principal focus.

parts.stem: State the other name used for a diverging lens.

scheme.for: concave

hints: It is the word that goes with the shape that curves inwards.
parts.workedSolution: Concave. A concave lens is thin in the middle and spreads parallel rays apart.

commonErrors.feedback: Convex is the fat-in-the-middle shape, which converges light. The diverging lens is concave.

parts.stem:
In a ray diagram a lens is drawn as a straight vertical line with arrowheads at each end.
State what the arrowheads on the symbol for a converging lens point.

options.text: outwards, away from the axis
options.feedback: Correct. Outward arrowheads mean converging; inward ones mean diverging.

options.text: inwards, towards the axis
options.feedback: Inward arrowheads are the diverging symbol.

options.text: along the axis, one each way
options.feedback: The arrowheads sit at the top and bottom of the line, not along the axis.

scheme.for: outwards

hints: The arrowheads copy the shape of the glass.
parts.workedSolution: Outwards. The symbol for a converging lens is a vertical line with its arrowheads pointing away from the axis; the diverging symbol has them pointing inwards.

parts.stem:
The diagram shows a converging lens standing on a horizontal line, with four features marked.
Name each of them.

scheme.for: (i) principal axis
(ii) optical centre
(iii) principal focus
scheme.examinerNote: Summer 2025 P2 Higher: many candidates were unsure where to label the focal point.

scheme.for: (iv) focal length

hints: One of the four is a distance rather than a place.
The centre of the lens sits where the lens meets the horizontal line.
parts.workedSolution: (i) principal axis — the horizontal line through the middle of the lens. (ii) optical centre — where the axis crosses the lens. (iii) principal focus — the point where parallel rays meet. (iv) focal length — the distance from the optical centre to the principal focus.

commonErrors.feedback: There is no normal and no image on this diagram. The four features are the principal axis, the optical centre, the principal focus and the focal length.

accepted: The distance from the optical centre of the lens to the principal focus.
It is the distance between the centre of the lens and the principal focus, where rays parallel to the axis meet.

scheme.for: the distance (threshold)
from the optical centre of the lens to the principal focus

hints: It is a distance, so say between which two things.
Name the point that parallel rays meet at.
parts.workedSolution: The focal length is the distance from the optical centre of the lens to the principal focus, the point where rays parallel to the principal axis meet.

parts.stem: Describe what a converging lens does to rays that arrive parallel to its principal axis.

accepted: It brings them together at the principal focus.
They are refracted so that they all meet at one point, the principal focus.

scheme.for: brings them together / they meet at the principal focus

hints: Say where the rays end up.
parts.workedSolution: It brings them together at the principal focus: every ray is refracted so that they all cross at the same point on the axis.

commonErrors.feedback: Spreading the rays apart is what a diverging lens does. A converging lens brings them together.

parts.stem: Describe what a diverging lens does to the same parallel rays, and say how its principal focus is found.

accepted: It spreads them apart, and the principal focus is found by tracing the spreading rays backwards until they cross.
The rays diverge, so you extend them backwards with dashed lines and the principal focus is where those lines meet.

scheme.for: the rays spread apart / diverge
the principal focus is where their backward extensions cross, on the same side as the incoming light

hints: The rays never actually meet, so how is the point found?
parts.workedSolution: It spreads them apart. They never meet, so the principal focus is found by tracing the spreading rays backwards with dashed lines until those lines cross, on the same side as the light came from.

parts.stem:
The five steps of the distant-object method for measuring the focal length of a converging lens are listed in the wrong order.
Put them in the order they should be carried out.

expectedOrder: Stand near a window and point the converging lens at a distant object outside.
Hold a white screen on the other side of the lens, in the shadow of the lens.
Move the screen backwards and forwards until the image on it is as sharp as possible.
Measure the distance between the lens centre and the screen with a metre rule.
Repeat the measurement twice more and take the mean of the readings that agree.

scheme.for: a distant object is used
the screen is moved until the image is sharp
the distance from the lens to the screen is measured
scheme.examinerNote: Summer 2025 P2 Foundation: most candidates earned one or more of the three marks, but few earned all three.

hints: Nothing can be measured until the image is sharp.
The mean comes last.
parts.workedSolution: 1. Stand near a window and point the converging lens at a distant object outside. 2. Hold a white screen on the other side of the lens, in the shadow of the lens. 3. Move the screen backwards and forwards until the image on it is as sharp as possible. 4. Measure the distance between the lens centre and the screen with a metre rule. 5. Repeat the measurement twice more and take the mean of the readings that agree.

scheme.examinerNote: A point contradicted elsewhere in the answer is not counted. The specialist words the scheme wants are distant object, parallel, sharp image, principal focus and focal length.

hints: Say what the object is and why it has to be distant.

parts.workedSolution: Point the converging lens at a distant object, such as a window across the room or a tree outside. Light from a distant object arrives at the lens almost parallel to the principal axis. Hold a white screen on the other side of the lens and move it backwards and forwards until the image on it is as sharp as possible. Then use a metre rule to measure how far the screen is from the centre of the lens. Parallel rays are brought together at the principal focus, so that distance is the focal length. Repeat the measurement and take the mean, leaving out any reading that is clearly out of line with the others.

parts.workedSolution: Lens B. Its focal length is 8.4 cm against 14.9 cm for lens A, so it brings parallel rays together in a shorter distance, which means it has bent each ray more.

prompts.prompt: How do you tell a converging lens from a diverging one, by shape and by symbol?
prompts.answer: A converging lens is fat in the middle and its symbol has arrowheads pointing outwards. A diverging lens is thin in the middle and its symbol has arrowheads pointing inwards.

prompts.prompt: What does a converging lens do to rays that arrive parallel to the principal axis?
prompts.answer: It brings them together at one point on the axis, the principal focus.

prompts.prompt: For a converging lens, define the focal length.
prompts.answer: The distance from the optical centre of the lens to the principal focus.

prompts.prompt: Where is the principal focus of a diverging lens, and how is it found?
prompts.answer: On the same side as the incoming light, where the backward extensions of the spreading rays cross.

prompts.prompt: Describe the distant-object method for measuring a focal length.
prompts.answer: Point the lens at a distant object, catch the image on a screen, move the screen until the image is sharp, and measure the distance from the lens to the screen with a metre rule.

prompts.prompt: Why does the distant-object method give the focal length rather than some other distance?
prompts.answer: Because light from a distant object arrives almost parallel, and parallel rays meet at the principal focus.

prompts.prompt: Four readings are taken and one is far from the other three. What do you do with it, and why?
prompts.answer: Leave it out of the mean, because it is anomalous and would pull the mean away from the true value.

prompts.prompt: Two converging lenses have focal lengths of 5 cm and 20 cm. Which bends light more, and what does that say about its shape?
prompts.answer: The 5 cm lens bends light more, and it is fatter in the middle.
